front_blocks.md: What does a **distance-time graph** show?

back_blocks.md: A **distance-time graph** shows how the** distance** of an object from a point changes over** time**.

back_blocks.md: A **horizontal line** on a **distance-time graph** represents an object that is not moving (it is **stationary**).

front_blocks.md: Define the **rate of change** of $y$ against $x$.

back_blocks.md: It is the amount that $y$ changes for every **1 unit of increase** in $x$, and on a graph it is measured by the **gradient**.
A **straight** line means that rate is constant, and a **horizontal** line means it is zero, so $y$ is not changing at all.

front_blocks.md: How do you work out the units of a gradient?

back_blocks.md: Divide the units on the $y$-axis by the units on the $x$-axis.
A graph of volume in cubic centimetres against time in seconds therefore has a gradient measured in cubic centimetres per second.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A rate-of-change graph must always have time on the horizontal axis.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Time is the commonest choice, but any two variables can be plotted against each other.
The volume of air in an inflating balloon plotted against its radius is a rate-of-change graph with no time on it at all.

front_blocks.md: A graph of fuel in litres against distance in kilometres has gradient $- 0 . 09$. What does that mean?

back_blocks.md: The units are litres per kilometre, so travelling **1 km uses up 0.09 litres** of fuel.
The gradient is negative because the amount of fuel left in the tank is **decreasing** as the distance increases.

front_blocks.md: What does the gradient of a tangent to a curved graph estimate?

back_blocks.md: It estimates the **rate of change at that particular point**, since the rate is no longer constant along a curve.
Where the curve is **steeper** the rate of change is greater, and the tangent's gradient is only an estimate because the tangent is drawn by eye.

front_blocks.md: Water flows at a constant rate into a container that gets narrower towards the top. What does its depth-time graph look like?

back_blocks.md: Its gradient starts **shallow** and becomes **steeper**, because the same volume of water each second fills a narrower space and so raises the depth more quickly.
A container with vertical sides would instead give a **straight** line, since the depth would rise at a constant rate throughout.

front_blocks.md: A straight-line graph is used to model fuel remaining against distance travelled. Why might that model not be realistic?

back_blocks.md: A straight line assumes fuel is used at a **constant** rate for the whole journey.
In practice the rate changes with speed, traffic and load, so a more realistic graph would be a curve.
